questions.q: List the four main supporting characters in "I Sell My Dreams" and state each one's primary function in the narrative in one sentence.
questions.a: The four main supporting characters are: (1) Frau Frieda — the dream seller whose prophecies drive the plot and embody the theme of survival through superstition; (2) The Viennese family — the collective patron who surrenders autonomy to Frau Frieda's dreams, representing institutionalized credulity; (3) Pablo Neruda — the rationalist poet who dismisses prophetic dreams, serving as a foil to Frau Frieda and a symbol of artistic intuition; (4) The Portuguese ambassador — the final witness who confirms Frau Frieda's lifelong role as a dreamer, validating her identity but also the ambiguity of her power. A wrong answer that omits the ambassador or conflates the family with Frau Frieda reveals failure to distinguish between active agents and passive recipients of the dream economy.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the Viennese family continues to employ and obey Frau Frieda even after the master's death, despite the narrator's suspicion that her dreams are a "stratagem for surviving."
questions.a: The family obeys Frau Frieda because their religious superstition makes them interpret her dreams as divine guidance, and her accurate prediction of the brother's death (via the caramel choke) established absolute authority. The master's will legally bound her to continue dreaming, transforming a survival tactic into a hereditary obligation. A wrong answer that attributes their obedience solely to fear or greed misses the textual evidence that they were "religious and therefore inclined to archaic superstitions" and "delighted to take in Frau Frieda" — showing willing participation, not coercion.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "foil" to analyze how Pablo Neruda's character highlights Frau Frieda's traits. Provide two specific textual contrasts.
questions.a: Neruda foils Frau Frieda in two key ways: (1) Epistemological stance — Neruda declares "Only poetry is clairvoyant," rejecting prophetic dreams, while Frau Frieda builds her livelihood on dream interpretation; (2) Physical/social presence — Neruda is described as a "Renaissance pope," gluttonous and commanding attention at the table, whereas Frau Frieda is marginal, "not pretty," aging prematurely, yet wields invisible power through dreams. A wrong answer that only notes they are "different" without linking to the story's theme of competing truth-claims (poetry vs. prophecy) shows surface-level understanding.

questions.q: Analyze the significance of the Portuguese ambassador's final statement: "In concrete terms... what did she do? 'Nothing,' he said... 'She dreamed.'" How does this exchange reframe the reader's understanding of Frau Frieda's agency?
questions.a: The ambassador's "Nothing... She dreamed" creates a deliberate paradox: socially, Frau Frieda did "nothing" (no conventional labor), yet her dreaming constituted total economic and psychological control over a household and later an ambassador's establishment. The disenchantment in his tone suggests even he — a rational diplomat — cannot fully dismiss her influence. This reframes her agency as soft power: she survived and thrived by monetizing the unverifiable. A wrong answer that takes "Nothing" literally misses the irony that her "nothing" was the most potent force in multiple households.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrator's reliability in portraying Frau Frieda. Does his admission that he considered himself "a survivor of some catastrophe I never experienced" enhance or undermine his credibility as a witness to her powers?
questions.a: The narrator's admission enhances his credibility because it demonstrates self-awareness about his own suggestibility — he acknowledges Frau Frieda's psychological impact on him without confirming her supernatural ability. This nuanced stance (neither full belief nor outright dismissal) makes him a more reliable observer of her effect on others. A wrong answer claiming he is "unreliable because he believed her" ignores his explicit skepticism ("I had always thought her dreams were no more than a stratagem") and his role as a critical chronicler, not a devotee.

questions.q: Create a 50-word character sketch of Frau Frieda from the perspective of the Viennese family's younger child (age 9 at first meeting). Focus on sensory details and emotional impact.
questions.a: She smells of boiled potatoes and old perfume. Her serpent ring flashes green when she tells Papa not to sign the contract. We wait at breakfast, spoons frozen, for her to say if today is safe. She never smiles, but sometimes she buys us pastries. We love her. We fear her. A poor answer would describe her physically (fat, old, ring) without capturing the child's lived experience of ritualized dependence, missing the story's core: how prophecy becomes domestic routine.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Supporting characters are secondary figures in a narrative who interact with the protagonist to advance the plot, reveal thematic concerns, or illuminate the protagonist's ______ through contrast or parallel.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're at a family wedding and notice a relative who barely speaks but everyone consults before making decisions — that's Frau Frieda in the Viennese ______.
What is Supporting characters? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Supporting characters are secondary figures in a narrative who interact with the protagonist to advance the plot, reveal thematic concerns, or illuminate the protagonist's personality through contrast or parallel.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Supporting characters?
questions.a: Students often treat Frau Frieda as either a genuine prophet or a conscious fraud.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) identify each supporting character's distinct role, motivation, and relationship to the narrator; (2) analyze how their dialogue and actions reveal the story's central themes of prophecy vs. rationality and survival vs. exploitation; (3) write a structured PEEL-paragraph answer comparing two supporting.
